CARRIED FROM the away.py cut: annotating a parameter as object and then passing it to float() grows by_code[arg-type] -- the untyped parameter hid the conversion. Narrow with isinstance before float, the same shape as wood_fuel._optional_float. Control: the first away.py pass with value: object then float(value) failed the arg-type ratchet; narrowing restored it and cleared the module. SCOPE OF THIS CARRY, because (a) once cited it for more than it shows: the float() call and the annotation are in the SAME module, so what it establishes is that an annotation RELABELS one by_code row into another at zero headroom. It says nothing about which FILE the relabelled error lands in, and cannot, because it never crossed one. The cross-file question is settled by (a)'s perturbation, and that one goes the other way. CARRIED FROM THE FIRST TAIL BATCH (this group), established by measurement with its control -- READ THIS BEFORE SIZING THE NEXT TRANCHE. THE TAIL IS BATCHED, NOT TAKEN ONE MODULE AT A TIME. With coordinator.py (W5-G4) and optimizer.py set aside, what remains is a couple of errors each across roughly thirty modules, so this group's one-module-per-pull-request convention is ceremony rather than review there. The rule, with the basis of each clause, because a precedent without its basis gets copied into cases it does not fit: (a) A BATCH IS WHOLE MODULES, NEVER A CODE SLICE ACROSS MODULES -- AND A MODULE IS NOT CLOSED BY CONSTRUCTION, SO THE by_module COMPARISON AT BOTH ENDS IS MANDATORY PER BATCH RATHER THAN A CONFIRMATION OF IT. Every by_code row is at zero headroom and a code the census never saw has a budget of zero, so a batch has to be CLOSED under the errors it creates: nothing outside it moves, in either direction. The module is the right UNIT because a by-code slice leaves modules half-annotated at zero headroom and finds out where it spilled only after the diff is drawn. THE UNIT IS NOT A GUARANTEE OF CLOSURE, and the first statement of this clause said it was -- it claimed that mypy attributes an annotation's downstream error to the module carrying the annotation. IT DOES NOT. mypy attributes an error to the file holding the offending expression, and for a parameter type the offending expression is the ARGUMENT AT THE CALL SITE, which can be in any module. A batch is closed only once it has been MEASURED closed. FAILURE MODE, with the perturbation that shows it -- re-run this, it is the control this clause now rests on, and it costs about six seconds under the pinned ruler: in dhw_draws.py change window_label(hour: float, windows: list[Window]) to windows: tuple[Window, ...], the ordinary immutable-sequence annotation for a parameter that is only iterated. Re-measured at the first tail batch's head df8b1a9: errors 197 -> 198, by_code[arg-type] 17 -> 18, 2 of 25 ruler checks FAILED, and by_module puts the new error in optimizer.py 58 -> 59 while dhw_draws.py stays at 0 -- the module carrying the annotation does not move and a module outside the batch does. mypy names the caller, the draw_window_label call in optimizer.py, where dhw_draws.window_label is imported under that alias -- anchored to the call and not to a line, because the two line numbers this sentence first carried were both falsified by the next merge from main. list[Window] was closed only because it happens to match what dhw_demand_windows declares in thermal_model.py; closure was a property of that match, not of the file boundary. THE SPILL IS ALSO SELECTIVE, WHICH IS WHY AN ARGUMENT CANNOT SUBSTITUTE FOR THE MEASUREMENT: the draw_window_label call inside coordinator.py's _async_fold_draw_stats passes the same parameter and does not move. Its argument reaches that line through the getattr fallback that binds ctx in _async_fold_draw_stats, and a mypy reveal-type probe inserted at that call prints Revealed type is Any -- an UNCHECKED caller, not a closed one, so one annotation spills into one consumer and not the other. The consumers that make a spill expensive are exactly coordinator.py (W5-G4's whole scope, and the largest by_module row, 89 at that head) and optimizer.py (58), both at zero by_code headroom like every other row; whether a batch reaches them is a fact about the annotations that batch chose, never about the file boundary. RE-MEASURE, DO NOT CARRY ANY OF THESE FIGURES: emit the pinned ruler's measurement at both ends (tests/typing_ruler.py --mypy --emit) and diff by_module key by key at your own merge base, and re-run the perturbation there rather than trusting this paragraph. (b) CHOOSE THE MODULES BY THE PROTOCOL THEY IMPLEMENT, not by their error count. A batch drawn on 'modules with N errors' hands the reviewer N unrelated arguments; a batch drawn on one protocol is one argument checked N times, and it has a property to test rather than a list to trust. (c) CAP THE BATCH AT THE LARGEST SINGLE-MODULE TRANCHE THIS GROUP HAS ALREADY MERGED. DERIVE THAT CAP, DO NOT CARRY IT: this group's merged commits on origin/main name both census endpoints in their own subjects, so the per-tranche deltas and their maximum are re-derivable from git log at your merge base, and they are a sliding window that decays if quoted. What the derivation showed is the point of the clause: the convention held the UNIT fixed and let the SIZE float several-fold, so size was never what it protected -- in the tail the unit collapses and only the ceremony survives, so hold the size and float the unit instead. CONTROL, and what a closed batch looks like once the comparison in (a) is actually run: the first batch took ten modules whole on the as_dict / from_dict / summary / load / from_config seam, and tests/typing_ruler.py's own by_module table showed those ten going to zero with no other module moving in either direction -- including coordinator.py and optimizer.py, which consume those dictionaries. That is a measured result about those ten annotations, not a property the file boundary conferred on them. Attribution is from the ruler's emitted by_module, never from a git-diff argument. Re-measure at your own merge base; tests/typing_budgets.json is what is pinned. WHAT THE RULE IMPLIES FOR THE REMAINING BATCHES, measured at that same merge base and to be re-derived rather than trusted: the next protocol is the Home Assistant platform-entity constructor, whose coordinator and entry parameters carry no annotation, in binary_sensor.py and button.py and their siblings; after that the numeric-coercion boundary, float() over a value typed Any or None off a state or a stored payload, whose narrowing shape is _optional_float in wood_fuel.py. Those two clusters plus this batch's protocol are most of the tail, and each is a batch under (b). A module no protocol claims is taken whole into the batch it is nearest, not made a pull request of its own. ORDER: the platform-entity batch STANDS AS THE NEXT ONE. The refutation in (a) does not reorder it, but it makes it conditional: run (a)'s by_module comparison rather than assume it. That batch is the shape most exposed to the spill in (a), because coordinator and entry are cross-module names; it does not in fact spill, and the reason is structural rather than lucky -- Home Assistant constructs a platform's entities in that platform module's own async_setup_entry from entry.runtime_data, so the callers of those constructors sit in the annotating file. MEASURED, BOTH MODULES, at df8b1a9 -- re-run before sizing the batch: annotating the five subclass __init__ signatures in binary_sensor.py with the coordinator and config-entry types gave errors 197 -> 192, by_code[no-untyped-def] 67 -> 62, by_module binary_sensor.py 5 -> 0 and NO other module moved; annotating the four in button.py gave errors 197 -> 193, by_code[no-untyped-def] 67 -> 63, by_module button.py 4 -> 0 and no other module moved. EXTENT OF THE BATCH, by measurement rather than by 'and their siblings': the bare def __init__(self, coordinator, entry) shape survives in exactly two modules at that head, binary_sensor.py and button.py, nine errors between them, and all nine ARE that constructor -- so both close whole. sensor.py already carries the annotated pair and is at 0. WHAT IS LEFT IN climate.py, switch.py, datetime.py and __init__.py IS A DIFFERENT PROTOCOL, NOT A DIFFERENT CODE, and an earlier draft of this block got that wrong: it said the eight errors there are no-any-return, name-defined and arg-type, and TWO OF THEM ARE no-untyped-def -- _lazy and _async_lazy, the two module-level lazy-import helpers declared near the top of the integration package's __init__.py. Both take a module name and return a module, they are not the platform-entity constructor, so the extent of the batch above is unchanged -- but do NOT read this group as having cleared no-untyped-def everywhere outside binary_sensor.py and button.py. The other six are no-any-return in __init__.py, switch.py and climate.py (twice), name-defined in datetime.py and arg-type in __init__.py. Re-derive the whole residue at your own merge base from the pinned ruler rather than carrying this list. NULL CONTROL on the structural claim, with its positive arm, because the control returns nothing. THE RULE, because a count with no rule beside it is not re-derivable and must not be inherited: parse every .py file under the integration package with ast.parse; the class set is every ast.ClassDef name in the six platform modules (sensor.py, binary_sensor.py, button.py, climate.py, switch.py, datetime.py); a construction site is an ast.Call whose func is an ast.Name naming one of those classes; a site is OUTSIDE when the file holding it is not the module that defines that class. Under that rule the load-bearing arm -- construction sites outside the owning module -- returns 0, and the positive arm, the same scan with the outside-only filter removed, returns a non-zero count every one of whose sites is inside the owning module, so the scan can find what it is looking for. RE-DERIVE BOTH ARMS with that rule at your own merge base and carry neither count. In particular the 151 an earlier draft of this block gave for the positive arm is WITHDRAWN: no ast construction scan produces it, and it is the shape of a text match on ClassName( which also counts class-definition headers, which are not constructions. If a later tranche constructs a platform entity from __init__.py or coordinator.py, this ordering stops being safe, and (a)'s comparison is the thing that would catch it.
